ONE_PRIMARY: Until now, every account has belonged to one Primary Database.
DIVIDE: Instead of keeping all accounts under that single owner, imagine dividing them into separate groups.
OWNER_A: One database group owns one set of accounts.
OWNER_B: Another database group owns a different set.
SHARD_DEF: A shard is a partition of the data with a defined owner.
INDEPENDENT_PRIMARY: And unlike read replicas, separate shards can have separate Primary instances responsible for their own accounts.
CRITICAL_LOOKUPS: If account lookups can be distributed across independent owners, the critical authentication work no longer has to reach the same Primary every time.
SHARD_A: A request for one account reaches Shard A.
SHARD_B: A request for another account reaches Shard B.
AUTHORITATIVE: Each shard performs its own authoritative account check.
SHARD_KEY_QUESTION: But how does Auth 01 know which shard owns an account?
SHARD_KEY_DEF: A shard key is information used to determine where a record belongs.
MAPPING: For our example, imagine that account routing uses a normalized Login identifier through a consistent mapping rule.
ROUTING: The database routing layer uses that identifier to find the correct shard.
IDENTIFIER_CHANGE: If the user changes that identifier, the system must still find the correct account.
MISSING_KEY: And if the query does not contain enough information to identify the owner, we may need an additional lookup or a query across multiple shards.
HOT_SHARD_QUESTION: What if one shard receives most of the traffic while the others are almost idle?
HOT_WARNING: Sharding only helps when the data and workload are distributed in a useful way.
CROSS_SHARD: It also makes account migration, cross-shard operations, and recovery more complicated.
EACH_REPLICAS: And each shard can still have its own replicas for availability and suitable reads.
COMPARE: So replication and sharding are not competing names for the same solution.
COMPARE_DEF: Replication creates copies of data. Sharding divides responsibility for data.
CAPACITY: For our Login example, sharding may let us distribute critical account lookups between multiple Primary owners.
HYPOTHESIS: But it is still a hypothesis until testing proves the complete Login journey can handle the additional demand.
FAILURE: What happens when one of those owners fails?
